Room data sheet template

A room data sheet is a concise requirements register. It brings together what is known about one room while keeping the source and status of each entry visible.

By OpenLintel · Updated September 15, 2026 · Educational resource

What each field records

Room
Stable room name or number.
Topic
Group geometry, use, constraints, or finishes.
Requirement / value
Record one clear statement per row.
Unit
Include units for numeric dimensions.
Source
Identify the brief, survey, or drawing.
Status
Distinguish nominal, proposed, and verified.
Action / owner
Name the next information request and responsible person when appointed.

How to use this template

Use one room identifier throughout the project. A requirements entry describes intent; a measured entry needs a survey source. Do not convert either into a verified technical specification merely by placing it in a spreadsheet. Check changed source information against all dependent documents before replacing the current room record.

  1. Assign the room reference before capturing requirements.
  2. Record the source and status alongside every important fact.
  3. Review open actions when the brief or survey changes.

Keep the source with the room requirement

Treat each row as a statement with provenance, not a container for a number. “The client wants storage” and “the wall is this long” need different evidence. A proposed dimension is not made verified by being copied into the room register.

When a new survey differs from a nominal source, keep the discrepancy visible until it has been resolved. Then update dependent drawings and schedules through an identified issue, rather than quietly replacing the number everywhere.

Review before use

  • A precise-looking number can still be nominal.
  • Do not mix requirements with verified performance results.
  • Do not duplicate a fact in several registers without a clear source of truth.

Units, source information, and US use

The worked example keeps its original nominal metric dimensions. For a US project, choose and label a primary imperial or metric convention, distinguish item counts from areas, and document any display conversion and rounding. Never relabel metric values as imperial or treat conversion as site verification.
